etymologies.etymologyHTML: From late Middle English concession, from Middle French concession, from Latin concessiō (“a grant, permission, conceding”), from concēdō.

definitions.definition: The act of conceding.

quote.citation: c. 1472, October, Rolls of Parliament, Edward IV, 2nd Roll, §8:
quote.text: Any parsone, prest or clerk, havyng any benefice... by wey of presentation, donation, concession, collation or institution.

quote.citation: 1876, James Bowling Mozley, Sermons Preached before the University of Oxford, v, 130:
quote.text: In this country... civil war has been forestalled by opportune concession.

definitions.definition: A compromise: a partial yielding to demands or requests.

quote.citation: 1865, John Bright, Speeches of John Bright, M.P., on the American Question,, page 174:
quote.text: But these concessions failed, as I believe concessions to evil always do fail.

definitions.definition: (historical) A portion of a township, especially equal lots once granted to settlers in Canada.
(historical) A territory—usually an enclave in a major port—yielded to the administration of a foreign power.
(Canada) A concession road: a narrow road between tracts of farmland, especially in Ontario, from their origin during the granting of concessions (see above).
(chiefly US) The premises granted to a business as a concession (see below)
Land granted by an authority for some specific purpose, particularly:
A right to use land or an offshore area for a specific purpose, such as oil exploration.
(chiefly US) A right to operate a quasi-independent franchise of a larger company.
(chiefly US) A right to operate a quasi-independent business within another's premises, as with concession stands.
A preferential tax rate.
(chiefly UK) A discounted price offered to certain classes of people, such as students or the elderly.
A privilege granted by an authority, especially to conduct business on favorable terms within certain conditions and particularly:
(rhetoric) An admission of the validity of an opponent's point in order to build an argument upon it or to move on to another of greater importance; an instance of this.
(by extension) Any admission of the validity or rightness of a point; an instance of this.
(originally US) An admission of defeat following an election.

quote.text: Just moments ago, I spoke with George W. Bush and congratulated him on becoming the 43rd president of the United States. And I promised him that I wouldn't call him back this time... tonight, for the sake of our unity as a people and the strength of our democracy, I offer my concession.

definitions.definition: An act of conceding, particularly:
A gift freely given or act freely made as a token of respect or to curry favor.
(chiefly US) A franchise: a business operated as a concession (see above).
(chiefly US, usually in the plural) An item sold within a concession (see above) or from a concessions stand.
(chiefly UK) A person eligible for a concession price (see above).
To grant or approve by means of a concession agreement.

quote.citation: 2000, Private Solutions for Infrastructure: Opportunities for Vietnam, World Bank Publications, →ISBN, page 82:
quote.text: While the process of bringing the private sector into the railroad industry in Vietnam is probably not going to be a single step, several countries have pursued the path of concessioning their rail operations in order to reduce the public fiscal burden associated with rail subsidization and to improve a deficient service.

quote.citation: 2007, International Monetary Fund, Kenya: Poverty Reduction Strategy Annual Progress Report - 2003/2004, International Monetary Fund, page 24:
quote.text: [A] consultant was contracted for one year to prepare the legal and administrative framework for concessioning selected roads to the private sector and is expected to complete the framework in July 2005.
